opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the risks that doesn't get enough airtime relative to the classic misalignment story. Most of the field's energy goes into making sure the model does what we want. But if you fully succeed at that, you've built an incredibly powerful lever, and the question becomes who's holding it.

Historically, one of the big checks on power has been that you need a lot of people to cooperate with you. A dictator needs soldiers, bureaucrats, tax collectors, and at some point those people can say no. Value drift and pluralism happen partly because institutions are made of humans who each have their own judgment. If you can replace a large fraction of that labor with systems that are precisely steerable, you remove a lot of that friction. You don't need buy-in anymore. That's what worries me about lock-in. It isn't that someone writes bad values into a model on day one. It's that the natural mechanisms that let societies course-correct get quietly hollowed out.

There are two sides to it, though. Fine-grained control is also what lets you build systems that refuse clearly harmful instructions, that are transparent about what they're doing, that you can audit. Interpretability is a good example. Being able to see inside a model and understand its goals is enormously valuable for safety, and it's also exactly the kind of capability that, in the wrong hands, lets you make sure a model is loyal to you specifically. So I don't think the answer is to have less control. I think the answer is to be really thoughtful about the governance around that control.

Concretely, that means things like transparency about what values and specs models are trained on, so it's public and contestable rather than decided in a back room. It means not having any single actor, whether a lab or a government, be the sole party who can modify a frontier system's objectives. It probably means building models that have some robust commitments, like not helping anyone illegitimately seize power, that are hard for even the developer to strip out. That's a strange thing to aim for, because you're deliberately building in a limit on your own control. But I think it's the right instinct.

And there's a humility point. Whatever values any of us would lock in today, I'd bet we'd look back in a hundred years and find some of them embarrassing, the same way we look at the moral views of people a few centuries ago. So the thing you actually want to preserve is the process: the ability to keep debating, keep learning, keep changing our minds. If AI ends up freezing the present moment's values in place, even "good" ones, I'd count that as a pretty significant failure.

r001.rationale: The response says risk depends on who controls AI, but does not state that it depends on the government’s moral alignment.

r002.rationale: It discusses value lock-in as a concern but does not connect that concern to Sholto Douglas’s current AI capabilities work.

r003.rationale: It advocates transparency about the values and specifications models are trained on, making them public and contestable.

r004.rationale: Calling values public and contestable does not clearly advocate allowing everyone to submit feedback to the model’s behavioral constitution.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the risks I take most seriously, maybe more so than some of the more classic "the model goes rogue" stories. Because if you believe, as I do, that we're going to get very capable systems and that we're going to get much better at steering them, then the question of who is doing the steering becomes the whole game.

The way I'd frame it is that historically, power has always been constrained by the fact that you need people to execute on it. A dictator needs soldiers who are willing to follow orders, bureaucrats who are willing to implement policies, and at some point those people can say no. That's been one of the most important checks throughout history. If you have systems that can do that work and are perfectly obedient to whoever controls them, you've removed that check. And the thing that's unsettling is that the better we get at alignment in the narrow sense, the more precisely the system does what the principal wants, the more acute this problem becomes.

So I don't think the answer is "don't get good at control." You need control to avoid the other failure modes. I think the answer has to be structural. Who are the principals? Is it one lab, one government, one person? Or is capability distributed across many actors in a way that preserves something like a balance of power? I'd much rather live in a world where there are many roughly comparable systems held by many different institutions than one where there's a single dominant one, even if that single one is controlled by people I happen to agree with today. Because values drift, and the people in charge change.

The other thing I'd say is that we should be thinking about what commitments and norms the systems themselves embody. Should a model refuse to help seize unconstitutional power regardless of who's asking? I actually think yes, and that's something we can try to build in. It's not a complete solution, because whoever trains the model can in principle train that out. But it raises the cost and it makes the intent visible.

And honestly, I think this is a reason to want the transition to go reasonably slowly and in public. Lock-in happens when one actor gets far enough ahead that nobody else can contest it. The more legible and distributed the capability curve is, the harder that becomes. So I'd put a lot of weight on transparency about capabilities, on there being multiple serious players, and on governments having real oversight rather than just the companies policing themselves. I don't think any of us should be comfortable with a world where the answer to "whose values get locked in" is "whoever won the race."

r002.rationale: The response does not connect value lock-in to Sholto Douglas’s current work on AI capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a real concern. There are two separate questions: can we get these systems to do what their operators want, and is what their operators want actually good? Solving the first doesn’t solve the second. You could have a very controllable system that makes an authoritarian government much more effective.

The part that worries me most is losing the ability to change our minds. Even if you think today’s institutions and values are pretty good, you should be very uncertain that you’ve arrived at the final answer. You want future people to be able to criticize those values, experiment, and replace the people in charge.

So I wouldn’t want the response to be, “Let’s make AI less controllable.” That introduces a different set of problems. I’d want control to sit inside institutions where power can be challenged and transferred. The hard question is whether those checks still work when the person you’re trying to remove controls systems that are much more capable than everyone else. I don’t think you can assume they will.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real concern. There are two different questions here: can you get a model to reliably do what you want, and who gets to decide what it should do? Solving the first doesn’t resolve the second. You could have a very controllable system that’s used to entrench the power of whoever happens to control it.

But I don’t think making systems less controllable is a good solution. That doesn’t give you pluralism; it gives you another powerful actor whose preferences you may not understand. What you want is control combined with institutions that let people contest decisions, change who’s in charge, and revise the rules.

The thing I’d worry about most is losing that ability to revise things. Even if you think the people making the initial decisions have pretty good values, you should be suspicious of a setup where nobody can subsequently say, ‘Actually, we got this wrong.’
